mainTopic: When a false oath counts as a mistake that brings a קרבן, and whether an oath needs spoken words (שמואל).
overview: רבא asks רב נחמן how a false oath about the past can ever be a mistake that brings a קרבן. If the person knew the truth, he lied on purpose, and if he did not know, he could not help it. רב נחמן answers that the person knew the oath was forbidden but did not know it requires a קרבן. Even the רבנן, who usually disagree with מונבז on this point, agree here, because a קרבן for a plain לאו with no כרת is unusual. Next, רבינא asks about a hungry man who forgot his oath and ate the loaf he swore off. רבא answers from a ברייתא that a קרבן comes only if knowing would have stopped him. Then שמואל rules that an oath decided in the heart must be said out loud. The גמרא defends this rule against two ברייתות. רב ששת rereads the first one, and the second, about the gifts to the משכן ('כל נדיב לב'), is shown to be a holy matter that cannot teach the rule for everyday oaths.

steps.title: How can a false oath about the past be unintentional?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what kind of case counts as a שוגג for a false שבועת ביטוי about the past. Both choices seem to fail.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is an unknowing false oath about the past? If he knew the truth, he sinned on purpose. If he did not know, he could not help it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks רב נחמן to describe a case where someone swears falsely about the past by mistake. He shows that both obvious options do not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A false oath about the past is about something that already happened. If the person remembered the facts, he is a מזיד, and a מזיד does not bring a קרבן. If he forgot the facts, he is an אנוס, and an אנוס is fully exempt. So there seems to be no middle case left for a שוגג.

keyTerms.meaning: An oath about yourself, like 'I ate' or 'I will eat'
An unknowing mistake that brings a קרבן
Someone who could not help it, so he is fully exempt

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up שוגג and אנוס. A שוגג made a mistake and brings a קרבן. An אנוס had no control at all and owes nothing.

phrases.english: What is the unknowing case of
an oath on an utterance about the past?
If he knows, he is acting on purpose!
If he does not know, he could not help it!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵיזוֹ הִיא שִׁגְגַת שְׁבוּעַת בִּיטּוּי לְשֶׁעָבַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the inquiry in this section.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A workable case of a שוגג in a false oath about the past, since both knowing and not knowing seem to rule out a קרבן.

steps.title: He knew it was forbidden but not that it requires a קרבן
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן explains that the case is someone who knew the oath was forbidden but did not know it requires a קרבן.
steps.simpleTranslation: He answered: It is where the person says, 'I know this oath is forbidden, but I do not know whether one must bring a קרבן for it or not.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן gives the middle case רבא was looking for. The person knew the oath was wrong, but he did not know about the קרבן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The mistake here is not about the facts. It is about the punishment. Because the person did not understand the full result of his act, he is called a שוגג and brings a קרבן.

keyTerms.meaning: One must bring a קרבן for it

phrases.english: He said to him: It is where he says:
'I know that this oath is forbidden,'
but I do not know

phrases.aramaic: אִם חַיָּיבִין עָלֶיהָ קׇרְבָּן אוֹ לָאו״.
phrases.english: whether one is liable to bring a קרבן for it or not.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The שוגג is someone who knew the oath was forbidden but did not know it requires a קרבן.

steps.title: Does this answer only work for מונבז?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks whether רב נחמן's answer only fits מונבז, who holds that not knowing about the קרבן counts as שגגה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who does this follow? Does it follow מונבז, who says that not knowing about the קרבן counts as an unknowing mistake?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on the answer. He suggests it only works according to one opinion, מונבז, and not according to the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מונבז and the רבנן argue about someone who knew an act was forbidden but did not know it requires a קרבן. מונבז calls him a שוגג, and the רבנן do not. If רב נחמן's case depends on מונבז, then according to the רבנן there would still be no case.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who argues with the רבנן about not knowing about the קרבן
Not knowing that an act requires a קרבן

phrases.english: Who does this follow? Like מונבז, who says:
phrases.notes: Their argument is found in מסכת שבת, 69a.

phrases.english: Not knowing about the קרבן counts as an unknowing mistake?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 2 by tying it to a minority opinion.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's case of not knowing about the קרבן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That case counts as שגגה only for מונבז. The רבנן disagree, so for them it would not work.

steps.title: Even the רבנן agree here, because this קרבן is unusual
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers that the רבנן disagree with מונבז only in ordinary cases. A קרבן for an oath is special, since no other plain לאו brings a קרבן.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can even say this follows the רבנן. They disagree with מונבז only for the rest of the תורה, where the קרבן is not unusual. But here it is unusual, because nowhere else in the תורה do we find a plain לאו that brings a קרבן.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן defends his answer. He says it can work even for the רבנן, because oaths are a special case. The next step finishes his explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a קרבן חטאת comes only for sins that carry כרת. An oath is just a plain לאו, yet it still brings a קרבן, which is something new. Because of this newness, the רבנן may agree that not knowing about this קרבן still counts as a real שגגה.

keyTerms.meaning: They only disagree in this case
Something new or unusual that breaks the normal pattern

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a legal argument can apply to ordinary cases and still not apply to an unusual one like this.

phrases.english: You can even say it follows the רבנן,

phrases.aramaic: עַד כָּאן לָא פְּלִיגִי רַבָּנַן עֲלֵיהּ דְּמוֹנְבַּז –
phrases.english: the רבנן disagree with מונבז only

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא בְּכׇל הַתּוֹרָה כּוּלָּהּ, דְּלָאו חִידּוּשׁ הוּא;
phrases.english: about the rest of the Torah, where it is not unusual;
but here, where it is unusual,
since in the whole Torah we do not find
a plain prohibition for which one brings a קרבן,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scope of the argument: the disagreement covers only ordinary cases, not this unusual one.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב נחמן's case works only according to מונבז.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even the רבנן can agree here, because a קרבן for a plain לאו is unusual.

steps.title: Why even the רבנן agree in the case of an oath
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן finishes his answer. Most קרבנות rules are learned from עבודה זרה, where a קרבן comes only for a sin punished by כרת. An oath brings a קרבן with no כרת, so even the רבנן agree here.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because we learn the rules of קרבנות from עבודה זרה. Yet here, with an oath, a person still brings a קרבן. So in this case even the רבנן agree.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן completes the answer from the last step. He explains why the oath's קרבן is so unusual that even the רבנן agree with מונבז about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a חטאת comes only for sins that carry כרת, a rule learned from עבודה זרה. A false oath has no כרת, but the Torah still requires a קרבן. Because this קרבן is so unusual, not knowing about it is enough to count as שגגה, even for the רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: Idol worship, the model case for the rules of the חטאת

steps.whatToRemember: The קרבן for a false oath is unusual because there is no כרת. So not knowing about the קרבן counts as שגגה, even according to the רבנן.

phrases.english: For we learn from idol worship;
phrases.notes: With עבודה זרה, doing it on purpose brings כרת and doing it by mistake brings a קרבן. Other sins follow that pattern.

phrases.english: and here he brings [a קרבן] –
even the Rabbis agree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the reasoning of רב נחמן's answer in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: the oath's קרבן is unusual, so the general dispute does not apply
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב נחמן's answer seemed to fit only מונבז.
steps.terutzMaskana: For an oath, even the רבנן agree that not knowing about the קרבן is enough for שגגה.

steps.title: רבינא's question: an oath on a loaf and a life in danger
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks רבא about someone who swore not to eat a certain loaf and is now in danger without it. What is the law?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא asked רבא: if someone swore about a loaf and is now in danger because of it, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic opens. רבינא asks רבא about a man who swore not to eat a loaf of bread and now his life is at risk if he does not eat it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether eating the loaf in this situation would make him owe a קרבן for breaking the oath. It sets up a discussion about what kind of mistake really counts as שגגה.

phrases.english: Ravina asked Rava:
If one swore about a loaf,
and he is in danger over it, what is the law?
phrases.notes: His life is at risk because he cannot eat the bread he swore off.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question about oaths and שגגה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a man who eats a loaf he swore off, when his life is in danger, owe a קרבן?

steps.title: רבא: in danger, he is simply allowed to eat
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects the question as asked. If the man's life is in danger, he is allowed to eat, so there is nothing to ask.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he is in danger, let the Master allow him to eat!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on the question. If the man's life is truly in danger, he may eat the bread, so this case cannot be the real question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saving a life overrides the oath. Someone who eats to save his life did nothing wrong and needs no קרבן, so the question must be about a different case.

keyTerms.meaning: The Master (a respectful way of saying "you")

phrases.english: In danger – let the Master permit him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the case described in the question of step 6.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The case of real danger to life
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: When life is in danger eating is allowed, so there is no sin and no question about a קרבן.

steps.title: The real question: suffering from hunger and forgetting the oath
steps.stepSummary: רבינא changes the case. The man is suffering, not in danger, and he ate the loaf because he forgot the oath. Does he bring a קרבן?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he is suffering, and he ate it while forgetting the oath. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא rewords his question. The man is very hungry but not in danger, and he ate the bread because he forgot about his oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His eating was a real mistake, but he was so hungry that he probably would have eaten even if he had remembered. The question is whether this still counts as a שגגה that brings a קרבן.

keyTerms.meaning: Suffering (from hunger), but not in danger
Forgetting about the oath (a mistake about the oath)

phrases.english: Rather, [the case is] he is suffering,
and he ate it forgetting the oath – what [is the law]?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected case from step 7 with a sharper one.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does someone who forgot his oath, but would have eaten anyway because of hunger, bring a קרבן?

steps.title: רבא answers: a קרבן only if knowing would have stopped him
steps.stepSummary: רבא quotes a ברייתא. A person brings a קרבן for a mistake only if knowing the truth would have stopped him. Here the man would have eaten anyway, so he does not bring one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: We learned in a ברייתא: if knowing would have made him stop, he brings a קרבן for his mistake. If knowing would not have made him stop, he does not bring a קרבן for his mistake.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers with a ברייתא. A mistake brings a קרבן only if the person would have held back had he known.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קרבן is for a real mistake, meaning the person did the act only because he did not know. The hungry man would have eaten even if he had remembered the oath, so his forgetting did not cause the act. That is why he brings no קרבן.

keyTerms.meaning: He would turn back if he knew

steps.whatToRemember: A קרבן comes only for a mistake that caused the act. If the person would have done it even while knowing, he brings no קרבן.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the man is excused because he was hungry. The ברייתא still calls his act 'שגגתו' (his mistake). He simply cannot bring a קרבן for it, because knowing would not have stopped him.
steps.whyThisMatters: This rule, that the person must be one who would have held back had he known, defines a true שגגה for all קרבנות.

phrases.english: He said to him: We have learned:
One who would turn back because of his knowledge –
phrases.notes: Literally "returns from his knowledge." He means: if he had known, he would have stopped.

phrases.english: brings an offering for his mistake;
one who would not turn back because of his knowledge –
does not bring an offering for his mistake.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the refined question of step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He does not bring a קרבן, since he would have eaten even if he had remembered the oath.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא: שב מידיעתו מביא קרבן, לא שב מידיעתו אין מביא קרבן

steps.title: An oath must be said with the lips
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that deciding on an oath in your heart is not enough. You have to say it out loud.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: If someone decided in his heart to swear, he still needs to say it with his lips, because the פסוק says 'to express with the lips.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a rule from שמואל: an oath only counts if it is spoken.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even a firm decision in the heart does not make an oath. שמואל learns this from the פסוק's words 'בשפתים' (with the lips), which point to actual speech.

keyTerms.meaning: He decided in his heart (made up his mind silently)
That he says it out with his lips

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule sets up the whole discussion that follows: is speech required for an oath, or can a decision in the heart be enough?

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
If one decided in his heart to swear,
he needs to say it with his lips,
as it says: "to express with the lips."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the case of the loaf in רבא's answer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath decided in the heart only counts once it is said with the lips.

steps.title: A ברייתא counts an oath decided in the heart
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that seems to say someone is liable even for an oath he only decided in his heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged him: 'With the lips' means not in the heart. Then how do we know about someone who decided in his heart? The פסוק teaches: 'whatever a person shall express with an oath.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks שמואל with a ברייתא. Its second half seems to say that an oath decided in the heart does count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל said a decision in the heart is not enough. The ברייתא uses a second phrase of the same פסוק to include 'one who decided in his heart.' That looks like the exact opposite of שמואל's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Whatever a person shall express with an oath (ויקרא 5:4)

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
"With the lips" means not in the heart.
From where do we know that one who decided in his heart is also included?
The verse teaches:
"Whatever a person shall express with an oath."
phrases.notes: ויקרא 5:4. This is the same פסוק as שמואל's source, just a different phrase from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's rule from step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's rule that an oath decided in the heart must be spoken.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא includes 'one who decided in his heart' as a valid oath, which goes against שמואל.

steps.title: The ברייתא seems to contradict itself
steps.stepSummary: Before dealing with שמואל, the גמרא points out that the ברייתא itself seems to say two opposite things.
steps.simpleTranslation: This ברייתא is difficult on its own terms. You said 'with the lips' and not in the heart, and then you said 'from where do we know one who decided in his heart?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to point out a problem inside the ברייתא. Its first line excludes the heart, and its next line includes the heart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first half says an oath in the heart does not count. The second half asks for a source to make an oath in the heart count. Both cannot be true about the same case, so the ברייתא must be talking about two different cases.

keyTerms.meaning: This source is difficult in itself (it contradicts itself)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new attack on שמואל. The גמרא is now asking about the ברייתא itself, which seems to say opposite things in back-to-back lines.

phrases.english: This ברייתא is itself difficult:
you said "with the lips" and not in the heart,
and then you said "from where do we know one who decided in his heart?"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns away from the challenge to שמואל and examines the ברייתא brought in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The internal consistency of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first line excludes an oath in the heart, while the second line includes one.

steps.title: Two different kinds of 'deciding in the heart'
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains that the ברייתא is describing two different cases, so it does not contradict itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: This is not difficult. This is what the ברייתא means: 'With the lips' excludes someone who decided in his heart to say the oath out loud but never said it. From where do we know about someone who simply decided in his heart? The פסוק teaches: 'whatever he shall express.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers the problem from step 12 by showing that each half of the ברייתא is about a different person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Case one: a person planned to say the oath out loud but never did, so there is no oath. Case two: a person simply decided the oath in his heart with no plan to speak it, and the פסוק 'whatever he shall express' includes him. The difference is whether he intended speech to be the act that makes the oath.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means to say

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב ששת's reading of the ברייתא, if a person planned to say an oath and never said it, there is no oath. If he simply decided it in his heart with no plan to speak it, he is included by 'לכל אשר יבטא.'

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: הָא לָא קַשְׁיָא;
phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said: This is not difficult.
This is what it means: "with the lips"
and not one who decided in his heart to say it with his lips
but did not say it.
From where do we know about one who simply decided in his heart?
phrases.notes: 'Simply' means he made the decision with no plan to ever say the oath out loud.

phrases.english: The verse teaches: "whatever he shall express."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: הָא לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each half of the ברייתא refers to a different kind of decision in the heart.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both lines of the ברייתא seemed to be about the same person, which made them contradict.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first line excludes one who planned to speak but did not. The second line includes one who simply decided in his heart.

steps.title: The ברייתא still seems to go against שמואל
steps.stepSummary: Now that the ברייתא no longer contradicts itself, the גמרא goes back to the original problem: it still seems to disagree with שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: But according to שמואל, it is still a difficulty!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the challenge it set aside in Step 12. The ברייתא now makes sense by itself, but it still seems to say that an oath decided in the heart counts, and that goes against שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת's answer in Step 13 only fixed the ברייתא's inner contradiction. It did not explain how the ברייתא fits with שמואל's rule that an oath must be said out loud. This line sets up a second answer from רב ששת.

keyTerms.meaning: But, however (turning back to the main question)

phrases.english: But according to שמואל, it is a difficulty!
phrases.notes: This is the question from Step 11 that the גמרא put on hold in Step 12. Now it comes back to it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the challenge against שמואל from Step 11, now that Step 13 has settled the ברייתא's inner contradiction.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's rule that an oath must be said out loud
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even read as two separate cases, the ברייתא still seems to make a man liable for something he only decided in his heart.

steps.title: רב ששת rereads the ברייתא so the words are always spoken
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains that the ברייתא is never about an oath made only in the heart. It is about a man who spoke an oath that did not fully match what he had in mind.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: Answer the question by reading the ברייתא like this. 'With his lips' teaches that he is not liable when he decided in his heart to say 'wheat bread' and actually said 'barley bread.' And if he decided in his heart to say 'wheat bread' and just said 'bread' without saying which kind, how do we know he is liable? The פסוק says: 'Whatever a person shall express.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת answers the challenge to שמואל by explaining the ברייתא differently. In both cases the man said words out loud. The only question is what happens when his words do not match his thoughts exactly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If his words and his thoughts are completely different (wheat in his heart, barley on his lips), the oath does not count. If his words are just less specific ('bread') and his heart fills in the detail ('wheat bread'), he is liable. The heart can explain spoken words, but it cannot replace them, so שמואל is right.

keyTerms.meaning: Will say out loud, will express

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the man in the 'bread' case swore only in his heart. He did say 'bread' out loud. His heart only explained which bread he meant.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רב ששת, thoughts can clarify the words of an oath, but there must always be spoken words. That is why the ברייתא does not go against שמואל.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said:
Answer it and read it like this:
'With the lips' – and not where he decided in his heart
to say 'wheat bread' and he said 'barley bread';
if he decided in his heart to say 'wheat bread'
and he said just 'bread,' from where do we know he is liable?
The פסוק says: 'Whatever a person shall express.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת, תָּרֵיץ וְאֵימָא הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against שמואל from Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the ברייתא so that every case in it involves spoken words
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to make a man liable for an oath he only thought about.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about spoken oaths. The heart can only add detail to unclear words, so שמואל stands.

steps.title: A second ברייתא: a decision in the heart counts
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges שמואל with a ברייתא that uses the words 'כל נדיב לב' to show that a decision made only in the heart counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged him: 'What comes out of your lips you shall keep and do.' From this I only know about a case where he said it with his lips. How do I know about a case where he only decided in his heart? The פסוק says: 'Everyone whose heart was generous.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא to challenge שמואל. This ברייתא says plainly that a decision made only in the heart makes a person obligated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק talks about what comes out of your lips, so the ברייתא asks how we know about a heart-only decision. It learns that from 'כל נדיב לב,' which says the people gave because their hearts moved them. If a heart-only decision makes a person obligated there, why not for an oath, against שמואל's rule that it must be spoken?

keyTerms.meaning: What comes out of your lips

phrases.english: They challenged: 'What comes out of your lips you shall keep and do'
I only know about a case where he said it with his lips;
how do I know about a case where he decided in his heart?
The פסוק says: 'Everyone whose heart was generous'!
phrases.notes: שמות 35:22. This is about the people bringing gifts for the משכן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first ברייתא was settled, the גמרא brings a new ברייתא against שמואל.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's rule that a decision in the heart alone is not enough
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says outright that a heart-only decision makes a person obligated, which seems to be the opposite of שמואל.

steps.title: Gifts to the משכן are a special case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the heart-only rule comes from a special פסוק about the משכן gifts, so it does not apply to oaths.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because it is written: 'Everyone whose heart was generous.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends שמואל. It says the ברייתא is only about a special area where the תורה itself says that the heart counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule that a heart's decision counts is not a general rule. The פסוק 'כל נדיב לב' teaches it for one specific setting, the gifts to the משכן. For oaths there is no such פסוק, so שמואל's rule that the words must be spoken still stands.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how a special rule learned from one פסוק stays in its own area and does not change the general rule for oaths.

phrases.english: It is different there,
because it is written: 'Everyone whose heart was generous.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the ברייתא in Step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the rule: a special פסוק makes this one area different
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A heart-only decision might count everywhere, even for oaths.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the משכן gifts have a פסוק that makes the heart count. Oaths still need spoken words, as שמואל says.

steps.title: Why not learn from the משכן gifts?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests: since a heart-only decision works for the משכן gifts, let us learn from there that it works for oaths too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let us learn from it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the last answer. If the heart-only rule exists for the משכן gifts, why not apply it to oaths as well?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 17 the גמרא said the heart-only rule comes from a special פסוק, so it does not apply to oaths. But a special פסוק could still be a model for other cases. So this short line challenges שמואל again: maybe we should copy the משכן rule over to שבועות.

keyTerms.meaning: And let us learn from it: a suggestion to apply one case's rule to another case

phrases.english: And let us learn from it!
phrases.notes: 'It' is the משכן gifts rule from the last step, applied here to oaths.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 17 by suggesting that the special פסוק should still serve as a model for oaths.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 17 that the heart-only rule is limited to the משכן gifts.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A rule written in one area of Torah can usually be extended to similar areas, so the heart-only rule should also apply to oaths, which goes against שמואל.

steps.title: Two פסוקים that say the same thing do not teach
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that both תרומה and קדשים have the heart-only rule. When two פסוקים teach the same thing, we do not learn from them to other cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because תרומה and קדשים are two פסוקים that teach the same thing, and any two פסוקים that teach the same thing do not teach it to other cases.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why we cannot copy the heart-only rule over to oaths. The rule shows up in two places, תרומה and קדשים, and that actually stops us from extending it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known rule called שני כתובין הבאין כאחד. If the Torah had to say the same thing twice, it is telling us the rule is limited to those cases. Otherwise one פסוק would have been enough and we could have learned the second case from the first. Per רש״י, the תרומה is the donations for the משכן, where 'כל נדיב לב' is written, and the קדשים are the עולות that 'כל נדיב לב' brought in חזקיהו's time (דברי הימים ב כט). So the heart-only rule stays with תרומה and קדשים and does not reach שבועות.

keyTerms.meaning: Two פסוקים that teach the same rule
They do not teach; we cannot extend the rule to other cases
Here, the donations for building the משכן
Here, the עולות brought willingly in חזקיהו's time

steps.confusionAlert: It sounds backwards: two sources make the rule weaker, not stronger. The reason is that if the rule could spread, the Torah would not have needed to write it twice.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a general rule of how we learn from פסוקים, and it comes up all over ש״ס.

phrases.english: Because תרומה and consecrated items are
two verses that come as one,
and any two verses that come as one
do not teach.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּהָווּ תְּרוּמָה וְקָדָשִׁים שְׁנֵי כְּתוּבִין הַבָּאִין כְּאֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 18 by explaining why the משכן rule cannot be extended to oaths.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A rule of learning from פסוקים (שני כתובין הבאין כאחד) blocks the comparison.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The heart-only rule of the משכן gifts could be applied to oaths.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since תרומה and קדשים both have this rule, it is limited to them and does not apply to oaths.

steps.title: What about the opinion that two פסוקים do teach?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that the last answer only works for the opinion that two such פסוקים do not teach. Some hold that they do teach.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works for the one who says they do not teach. But for the one who says they do teach, what can be said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the answer in step 19 is not accepted by everyone. It asks how שמואל's view would be defended according to the other opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a מחלוקת about שני כתובין הבאין כאחד. One opinion says they do not teach, and another says they do. According to the second opinion, step 19's answer falls apart and the challenge of step 18 comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: This works well (according to one opinion)
According to the one who says
What can be said? (the answer does not work for this opinion)

phrases.english: This works well according to the one who says they do not teach,
but according to the one who says they do teach –
what can be said?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנִיחָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר אֵין מְלַמְּדִין, אֶלָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר מְלַמְּדִין מַאי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the answer of step 19 to only one side of a מחלוקת.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer of step 19, which relies on 'אין מלמדין'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since some opinions hold that two such פסוקים do teach, the heart-only rule could still spread to oaths according to them.

steps.title: We do not learn חולין from קדשים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that oaths are everyday matters (חולין), while the משכן gifts (תרומה) and the offerings (קדשים) are holy. We do not learn rules for everyday matters from rules for holy matters.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are חולין and קדשים, and we do not learn חולין from קדשים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives an answer that works for everyone. Oaths belong to the everyday world and the heart-only cases belong to the holy world, so one cannot be learned from the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if two פסוקים can teach, they can only teach to similar cases. Holy matters have special rules that do not carry over to everyday matters. So the heart-only rule of קדשים does not apply to oaths, and שמואל's view stands.

keyTerms.meaning: We do not learn (one from the other)

steps.whatToRemember: The heart-only rule of 'כל נדיב לב' stays with holy matters (the משכן gifts and the offerings in חזקיהו's time). It cannot be applied to oaths. First reason: two פסוקים that say the same thing do not teach. Second reason, which works for everyone: we do not learn חולין from קדשים. So שמואל's view, that an oath only in the heart does not count, stands.
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes the challenge from 'כל נדיב לב' and protects שמואל's rule that an oath needs spoken words.

phrases.english: They are non-sacred matters and consecrated matters,
and we do not learn non-sacred matters from consecrated matters.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָווּ חוּלִּין וְקָדָשִׁים, וְחוּלִּין מִקֳּדָשִׁים לָא גָּמְרִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 20 with a reason that works even for the opinion that two פסוקים do teach.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The two cases belong to different categories (חולין and קדשים), so one cannot be learned from the other.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: According to 'מלמדין', the heart-only rule could extend to oaths.
steps.terutzMaskana: Oaths are חולין and cannot be learned from קדשים, so heart-only decisions do not make an oath according to any opinion.
